background.definition: Major depression is a clinical syndrome characterized by core symptoms of depressed mood and/or diminished pleasure lasting at least 2 weeks. The illness causes significant distress and/or occupational, social, or other impairment that is a change from previous functioning. The core symptoms and treatment duration are unchanged from DSM-IV-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 4th edition, Text Revision).

list.listitem: Based on the 2019 National Health Interview Survey, 4.7% of the general adult population has regular feelings of depression (CDC).
From 2013-2016 data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 8.1% of adults 20 years and over reported depression in any 2-week period.

In the 2018 National Ambulatory Medical Care Survey, 10.6% of US primary care office visits had depression indicated in the medical record, which is slightly higher than in the previous survey. CDC data show 10% of all emergency department visits were made by patients with diagnosed depression.

Depression is increased in populations with comorbid illness; for example, depressive symptoms are found in half of newly diagnosed patients with schizophrenia and 33% of people with chronic schizophrenia who have relapsed. Among 220 patients with stroke at 5-year follow-up, the prevalence rate of depression was 33%. Chronic pain conditions such as arthritis are associated with depression.

Suicide is the 10th leading cause of death the US. In 2020, there were 46,000 suicides in the US, which is 14 suicide deaths per 100,000 people. In addition, an estimated 12 million adults seriously considered suicide, over 3 million made a suicide plan, and 1.2 million people attempted suicide. The suicide prevalence was actually higher the prior year with 47,500 suicides, representing a 2% improvement from 2019 to 2020.

During the Covid-19 pandemic, mental illness burden has dramatically risen. Based on US Census Bureau Household Pulse Survey data, CDC reported significant increases from August 2020-February 2021 in symptoms of anxiety and depressive disorders among adults, with the largest increases among adults under 30 years and among those with less than a high school education. During the pandemic, about one third of high school students reported poor mental health, with pediatric emergency department visits for mental health conditions increasing especially for adolescent girls. About half of health care workers reported symptoms of depression or related mental health conditions.

According to the 2011 MMWR report using 2003 data, mental illness costs $100 billion in associated medical care annually, $24 billion in disability benefits, and $193 billion in lost productivity annually in United States.

Using national survey and administrative claims data from 2005-2010, investigators found a 21.5% increase in incremental economic burden for individuals with MDD, from $173.2 billion to $210.5 billion; approximately 45% was attributable to direct costs, 5% to suicide-related costs, and 50% to workplace costs. Just over one third (38%) of total costs was due to MDD as opposed to comorbid conditions.
For patients, a mood disorder diagnosis independently accounted for $6,591.60 in additional annual healthcare spending based on data from the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (2007-2017).
Higher utilizers of medical resources are more likely to have major depression.
Projected to become world's second largest cause of disability by 2030.
Globally, mental and substance use disorders account for 183.9 million disability-adjusted life years; depressive disorders account for about 40% of these.
Increases susceptibility to general medical conditions such as coronary artery disease and diabetes mellitus complications.
Increases risk of falls in depressed elderly (incidence rate ratio 1.6; 95% CI: 1.2-2.3).

In a VA database study, patients with depression and no known cardiovascular disease who were treated for 12 or more continuous weeks with any antidepressant had reduced risk of myocardial infarction (hazard ratios ranging from 0.34 to 0.48) and lower all-cause mortality (hazard ratios ranging from 0.5 to 0.66) than those treated for 11 or fewer weeks.
Stressful life events (e.g., divorce, widowhood, severe illness, job loss).
Childhood adverse experiences (e.g., excess criticism, rejection, neglect, abuse).
Dysfunctional attitudes, low self esteem.
Personality traits inhibiting satisfactory social functioning (e.g., excessively critical, judgmental, or pessimistic).
Environmental factors (e.g., natural disaster, discrimination, poverty).

Findings associated with depression include: Defects of serotonin activity (e.g., decreased production, release) and postsynaptic serotonin receptor abnormalities. Brain morphology and cellular deficits (e.g., reduced neural connections, glial cell size, cerebral blood flow, blunted amygdala hemodynamic activity to positive stimuli) observed via postmortem and in vivo imaging studies.
Increased corticotropin-releasing hormone and vasopressin secretion from hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis.
Increased proinflammatory cytokine (e.g., IL-6) secretion.
Cytokine-driven intrinsic apoptosis factors are associated with poststroke depression.

list.listitem: The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends screening adults, including pregnant and postpartum women, and adolescents (12-18 years) for depression in clinical practices with systems to assure effective diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. B
The USPSTF found insufficient evidence for screening children aged 11 years and under for depression.
There is no significant difference in performance of screening instruments, so pick a tool most practical for your clinical setting. B

Two-question screening is accurate (sensitivity 92%, specificity 68%; good for ruling out depression if both negative and if positive, assess for depression). One must screen 110 primary care patients to produce one additional remission after 6 to 12 months of treatment.
Depression can be detected in patients with dementia using validated tools such as the Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia and the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale.
The Patient Health Questionnaire 9 (PHQ-9) is commonly used. There is a modified version to use with teenagers called PHQ-A.

Behavioral interventions in high-risk groups may reduce the incidence of depression. For example, women who receive a psychosocial or psychological intervention in the prenatal or postpartum period are significantly less likely to develop postpartum depression compared with those receiving standard care (average RR 0.78, 95% CI: 0.66-0.93; 20 trials, 14,727 women). Promising interventions included individualized postpartum home visits by public health nurses or midwives, peer-based telephone support and interpersonal psychotherapy.
A web-based guided self-help intervention vs. enhanced usual care reduced the incidence of MDD over 12 months (27% vs. 41%) in patients with subthreshold depression.

Cognitive behavioral therapy or interpersonal therapy were associated with lower risk of perinatal depression in higher-risk women (such as women with a history of depression low income, single mothers or recent intimate partner violence).

In an RCT of 316 adolescents whose parents suffered from depression, a cognitive behavioral prevention program significantly reduced the onset of depressive episodes over 33 months compared with usual care (36.8% vs. 47.7%, respectively). The program consisted of 8 weekly 90-minute group sessions followed by 6 monthly continuation sessions.

Authors of a Cochrane review of evidence-based psychological prevention programs for children aged 5 to 19 years found small positive benefits for both self-rated depressive symptoms post-intervention and depression diagnosis up to 12 months (NNT 11). However, the authors caution that given the relative lack of evidence for universal interventions compared with attention placebo controls and the poor results from well-conducted effectiveness trials of universal interventions, there is not enough evidence to support the implementation of depression prevention programs.
High adherence to a Mediterranean diet is consistently associated with reduced risk for depression (relative risk [RR] 0.68; 95% CI: 0.54-0.86) as well as other brain diseases.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 49 studies with 266,939 individuals concluded that individuals with a higher level of physical activity, defined as more than 150 minutes per week of at least moderate-intensity activity, had a lower incidence rate of depression than those with low physical activity (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 0.83; 95% CI: 0.79 - 0.88).

Vitamin D supplementation does not reduce the incidence or recurrence of depression based on an RCT of 18,353 adults, 50 years or older, who had no clinically-significant depressive symptoms at baseline.
Best diagnostic tool for MDD is a detailed history performed by clinician in context of DSM-5 criteria and clinical judgment. C
Most prominent characteristics are depressed mood and/or decreased interest or pleasure. C
Symptoms cause clinically significant distress and represent clear change from previous functioning. C
DSM-5 no longer excludes individuals from receiving a diagnosis of MDD within two months of a significant death. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Persistent depressive disorder (previously called dysthymia and including chronic major depression)
Differential.Differential_Features: Requires only 3 to 4 depression symptoms, minimum symptom duration at least 2 years; core symptom must be depressed mood
Requires episodic abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood lasting at least 1 week
Requires documentation of specific cyclic symptoms associated with the luteal and menstrual phases of the menstrual cycle and evidence of dysfunction
Requires minimum 2 years with numerous periods depressive symptoms and numerous periods hypomanic symptoms, none meeting criteria for major depressive or manic episode
Focused history questions; consider toxicology screening if intoxication is suspected
Onset during winter months with low sun exposure

list.listitem: Defined in DSM-5:
Depressed mood or markedly diminished interest/pleasure most of day, nearly every day for ≥2-week period.

During this period, patient must also have at least four of the following symptoms nearly every day: significant weight loss/weight gain or appetite decrease/increase, insomnia/hypersomnia, psychomotor agitation/retardation, fatigue/loss of energy, feelings of worthlessness/excessive guilt, decreased concentration/indecisiveness, recurrent thoughts of death/suicidal ideation.
Episode must not be better accounted for by schizoaffective disorder, or superimposed on schizophrenia, schizophreniform disorder, delusional disorder, psychotic disorder NOS.
There has never been a manic, hypomanic, or mixed (manic/depressive) episode.
Symptoms are not the physiological result of a substance or a general medical condition.
Symptoms are not because of bereavement (see Differential Diagnosis).
Symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning.
Symptoms represent a change from previous functioning.

Most prominent characteristics are depressed mood and/or decreased interest or pleasure in activities. Most patients also experience problems with sleep, fatigue, restlessness, guilt/worthlessness, and poor concentration.
Symptoms represent clear change from previous functioning, and cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other functioning.
Best diagnostic tool is a detailed history performed by a practitioner in context of DSM-5 criteria and clinical judgment. See below for clinical decision rules that can be helpful in diagnosis.
As appropriate, evaluate for traumatic brain injury, intimate partner violence, trauma, or grief.
Rule out anemia with a complete blood count.
Rule out hypothyroidism with a TSH level.
Rule out substance use with history or toxicology screen.
Perform assessment for malignancy, sleep apnea and other sleep disorders, coronary disease, or rheumatologic conditions as indicated, based on history.
Screening tests with two questions and ten questions have been well validated and are recommended for primary care practice.
A tool for screening in the elderly has also been validated.

Depression screens of elderly patients in the hospital setting do not perform well. Even use of a scale specifically designed for hospitalized patients (the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale) performed poorly for diagnosing depression (area under the ROC curve 0.65, where 0.5 is non-informative and 1.0 is a perfect test), regardless of cognitive status.
The risk of suicidal ideation can be determined from a validated clinical rule.
A tool for screening postpartum patients for postpartum depression has been validated.
See algorithm in .

Implement antidepressant medication only after considering the following factors: clinical history, symptom severity, risk of suicide, expected side effects, patient preference, cost/availability (see and ). NICE guidance (UK) recommends offering patient-centered care and enlisting the family and caregivers in the treatment plan when possible. All patients should receive stepped therapy. For those with mild to moderate or persistent "subthreshold" depression, low-intensity psychological interventions and medication are options. For those who do not respond to initial therapy or who present with more severe depression, they recommend medication, high intensity psychological therapy (and possibly both) as well as referral for further assessment. Those with severe or complex depression, showing signs of self-neglect or at risk of suicide should also be considered for crisis referral, inpatient care, and/or electroconvulsive therapy.
It is unknown whether antidepressants are safe or effective for treating postnatal depression.
A shared decision-making tool can be used to select a medication, such as the one by Mayo Clinic.

Prescribing based on pharmacogenomic testing for drug-gene interactions for adults with MDD had no significant effect on symptom remission rates compared with the usual care group at 6 months based on an RCT with 1944 subjects.

listitem.strong: Antidepressants for initial therapy for MDD

strong.em: Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs)

list.listitem: Both TCAs and SSRIs are effective, compared to placebo, for depression treated in primary care settings. The number needed to treat (NNT) for TCAs ranges from 7 to 16 and for SSRIs from 7 to 8. The number needed to treat to harm (NNTH for withdrawal due to side effects) ranged from 4 to 30 for TCAs and from 20 to 90 for SSRIs. Due to better tolerability, SSRIs are more commonly used as first-line treatment.

Most commonly used antidepressants have similar reported efficacy and safety; SSRIs have equal efficacy and safety when compared to each other and to TCAs, venlafaxine, and bupropion. Although there are reported differences within classes of medications, findings are of limited trustworthiness due to potential for overestimation of treatment resulting from sponsorship bias and publication bias. In addition, authors of a Cochrane review note that use of an active placebo (one that mimics some antidepressant side effects) reduces effect sizes (which still favor antidepressant therapy [pooled effect size 0.39; 95% CI: 0.24-0.54]).

Higher doses of SSRIs may be slightly more effective in patients with MDD based on a meta-analysis of 40 RCTs. This benefit plateaus at around 250 mg of imipramine equivalents (50 mg of fluoxetine) and higher doses are associated with increased dropouts due to side effects.
Lesser recognized side effects from SSRIs include akathisia and sexual dysfunction that may be severe and enduring.

Antidepressant medication trials typically require 4 to 8 weeks at a given dose (see ). However, only one third to one half of patients respond to first medication used regardless of which class is selected.

It is important to allow an adequate treatment trial. Authors of a meta-analysis of individual patient data from 30 studies of treatment of severe major depressive disorder found that approximately one third of patients who do not show a medication response by 2 weeks will respond by 6 weeks.
Subtype of depression (e.g., anxious, melancholic) does not appear to predict response to antidepressants.

Investigators for the Sequenced Treatment Alternatives to Relieve Depression (STAR*D) trial of depression treatment in primary care found that only 28% of patients started on citalopram experienced remission after 12 to 14 weeks. An additional 30% achieved remission after additional treatment (new monotherapy, additional medication, new or addition of cognitive behavioral therapy), regardless of the treatment selected.

In a study of major depression treatment in daily practice in the Netherlands, investigators found a remission rate from initial medication of 27%, similar to the rate reported by the STAR*D trial and lower than remission rates reported in meta-analyses of RCTs (34%-47%).

In an attempt to better understand pharmacologic treatment in primary care, UK investigators randomized 655 primary-care patients with depressive symptoms of any severity or duration in the past 2 years, and for whom there was clinical uncertainty about antidepressant benefit, to sertraline or placebo. Among the 550 patients who remained in the study (similar attrition rates by group), there was no difference between groups in depressive symptoms at 6 weeks, possible differences in depressive symptoms at 12 weeks, and reduced anxiety symptoms, better mental (but not physical) health-related quality of life, and self-reported improvements in mental health for patients in the sertraline group.

Reevaluate effectiveness at least monthly until symptom remission (see ); if symptoms have not remitted after 4 to 8 weeks on given regimen, adjust treatment as indicated by the clinical situation (see ). All antidepressant classes are equally effective at inducing remission following treatment failure with another class (see ).
In one study, patients with depression accompanied by somatic symptoms had lower remission rates to medications than patients without somatic symptoms (for SSRIs 31% vs. 43%, respectively).
All antidepressant classes prevent relapse and recurrence during continuation and maintenance phases (see and ).

While some data indicate patients discontinue TCAs due to side effects more often than SSRIs, other data indicate they are similarly tolerated, TCAs are as effective in low as high doses, with less treatment discontinuation due to side effects at lower doses.

Discontinuation of SSRIs has been associated with a withdrawal reaction (i.e., antidepressant treatment discontinuation syndrome) that includes sensory, gastrointestinal-related, somatic, and psychiatric symptoms.

In a large database study in the UK, the tetracyclic drug mirtazapine (Remeron) and the selective serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor venlafaxine (Effexor) were associated with higher rates of completed suicide in primary care patients than other antidepressants (one-year absolute suicide risk ranged from 0.02% for amitriptyline to 0.19% for mirtazapine). There was no difference in suicide rates between SSRIs and TCAs, as shown in other studies.

Vilazodone, a selective serotonin 1A receptor partial agonist and reuptake inhibitor, was found to be more effective than placebo for response rate at 8 weeks (44% vs. 30%); however, remission rates were not significantly different than placebo on either of two depression scales. Common side effects were diarrhea, nausea, and headache.

In a Cochrane review of 5 trials in non-psychotic depression (unipolar or bipolar), there was a significant difference favoring treatment with antiglucocorticoids (e.g., mifepristone, ketoconazole, metyrapone and DHEA) over placebo (HAM-D 50% reduction: RR 0.72; 95% CI: 0.56-0.91). Across all mood disorders, there was no significant difference in the overall proportion of patients responding to these drugs over placebo.

In patients with MDD associated with subthreshold hypomanic symptoms (mixed features), the atypical antipsychotic lurasidone was more effective than placebo for depressive symptoms and overall illness severity. Few discontinued the drug due to adverse effects and rates of side effects (nausea 6.4% and somnolence 5.5%) were low.
In men with treatment-resistant depression, high-dose testosterone was associated with significant depression improvement.

listitem.strong: Combined pharmacologic agents or adjunctive therapy

list.listitem: In patients with treatment-resistant depression, antidepressant medications may be augmented with thyroid hormone or benzodiazepines (the latter for patients with prominent anxiety symptoms and only during the early treatment phase) (see and ). Other choices include cognitive behavioral therapy or aripiprazole.

Among adults with MDD who are unresponsive to an initial antidepressant medication, augmentation with aripiprazole (Abilify) is significantly better than switching to bupropion (Wellbutrin) monotherapy, but not better than augmentation therapy with bupropion.
Alprazolam (benzodiazepine anxiolytic) appears to reduce depressive symptoms more effectively than placebo and similarly to TCAs, but study quality is poor.

Second-generation antipsychotic drugs have also been shown to be effective in antidepressant augmentation but may be associated with weight gain (aripiprazole, olanzapine, risperidone) or sedation (quetiapine).

In a Veterans' Affairs hospital system study of adults with MDD unresponsive to an initial antidepressant medication, augmentation therapy with aripiprazole was significantly better than switching to bupropion monotherapy (28.9% vs. 22.3%, respectively), and similar to augmentation therapy with bupropion (26.9%).

In one RCT of 153 adults with moderate depression, the addition of B vitamins cyanocobalamin, thiamine, and folate to citalopram increased the percentage of patients in remission after 1 year (85.5% vs. 75.8% in the group without B vitamins), although vitamin supplementation did not influence initial response rate (78% of patients in both groups). Of note, remission rates were quite high and this group of patients had more severe depression than typically seen in primary care settings.

In a Cochrane review of 5 trials in non-psychotic depression (unipolar or bipolar), there was a significant difference favoring treatment with antiglucocorticoids (e.g., mifepristone, ketoconazole, metyrapone and DHEA) over placebo (HAM-D 50% reduction: RR 0.72; 95% CI: 0.56-0.91). Across all mood disorders, there was no significant difference in the overall proportion of patients responding to these drugs over placebo.

listitem.strong: Patients with Persistent Depressive Disorder (new term for dysthymia in DSM5)

list.listitem: Antidepressants, including TCAs, SSRIs and monoamine oxidase inhibitors are effective in the treatment of persistent depressive disorder over placebo with a NNT of about 5. Cochrane authors found no differences between and within drug classes (see chapter on Persistent Depressive Disorder).

In patients with both depression and psychosis, authors of a Cochrane review found that combination antidepressant plus an antipsychotic was more effective than antidepressant monotherapy (three RCTs; RR 1.49; 95% CI: 1.12-1.98), antipsychotic monotherapy (four RCTs; RR 1.83; 95% CI: 1.40-2.38) or placebo (two identical RCTs; RR 1.86; 95% CI: 1.23-2.82); risk of bias was high.
Olanzapine plus SSRI is superior to SSRI alone for preventing relapse in patients with psychotic depression.

In one RCT of 269 patients with psychotic depression treated with sertraline plus olanzapine for 12 weeks, 125 (46%) experienced remission or near remission for 8 weeks. Among these patients, those randomized to continued combined therapy vs. sertraline alone for 36 weeks had much lower relapse rates (20.3% vs. 54.8%, NNT= 2.9; 95% CI: 2.1-5.6). Adverse effects, primarily weight gain, were higher in the combined treatment group (17.2% vs. 4.8%), although there were similar rates of akathisia and tardive dyskinesia.

In patients with coronary heart disease (CHD) and depression, the use of SSRIs improved depression but had no impact on mortality or CHD readmission rates compared to controls. A Cochrane review supports psychological and pharmacological interventions with SSRIs for improving depression outcomes in patients with CAD but also found no beneficial effects on the reduction of mortality rates and cardiac events. There is specific evidence supporting escitalopram in patients with depression and acute coronary syndrome; it lowers all-cause mortality, recurrent MI, and PCI rates.

In patients with chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and depression, 18 months of treatment with escitalopram compared with placebo did not significantly reduce all-cause mortality or hospitalization, and there was no significant improvement in depression.

In an 8-year follow-up of a 24-week RCT of 300 patients with acute coronary syndrome and depression, those randomized to escitalopram had a significantly lower incidence of a composite of all-cause mortality, recurrent myocardial infarction, and percutaneous coronary intervention than the placebo group (40.9% vs. 53.6%, respectively; NNT = 7.9; 95% CI: 4.2 - 71.0). Patients whose depression had resolved also had a lower incidence of the composite outcome. In a subgroup analysis, there was no difference between the escitalopram group and the placebo group among patients with an ejection fraction <55% at baseline.
In patients with stroke, SSRIs were effective in preventing post-stroke depression.
In patients with depression and Parkinson's disease, nortriptyline was more effective than placebo or sustained release paroxetine.

In patients with multiple sclerosis and depression, two small RCTs found a trend toward efficacy with desipramine or paroxetine, but both trials had significant loss to follow-up and missing data; treatment side effects were common, especially nausea and headache with paroxetine.

It is unclear whether treating depression in patients with dementia or schizophrenia is of benefit. In patients with depression and dementia, there is little to no difference for use of antidepressants vs. placebo, especially beyond 12 weeks, and rates of adverse events are higher for those randomized to antidepressants.
Authors of a systematic review found a possible excess morbidity and limited evidence of benefit in critically-ill patients taking SSRI/serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors.
Cannabis: has not been shown to be effective for treatment of depression, anxiety, psychosis, ADHD or PTSD (large number of low quality studies).

Psilocybin: A trial randomized 59 adults with depression and no history of psychosis or personality disorder to 2 doses of 25 mg of psilocybin 3 weeks apart plus 6 weeks of daily placebo or 2 doses of 1 mg of psilocybin 3 weeks apart plus 6 weeks of daily oral escitalopram 10 mg. Both groups had a similar reduction in depression scores, and patients in the psilocybin group had a numerically greater likelihood of treatment response (70% vs 48%, p = 0.06).

St John's wort: insufficient evidence to determine efficacy as studies are heterogeneous; some studies demonstrated efficacy equal to SSRIs and TCAs, while others showed lack of efficacy; in meta-analysis, 71% of trials (10/14) were positive.
S-adenosyl methionine (SAM-e): data are conflicting regarding efficacy.
Saffron stigma and petal: has efficacy over placebo and similar efficacy to fluoxetine.
Lavender as an adjunct to imipramine (vs. imipramine alone) and Rhodiola (vs. placebo): also appear effective.
Folate: limited evidence supports role in medication augmentation.
Tryptophan and 5-hydroxytryptophan: limited evidence suggests greater efficacy than placebo.
DHEA: limited evidence of efficacy in short term studies only; may stimulate endometrial growth.

Acupuncture: insufficient evidence to determine efficacy. However, in an RCT with 270 patients with depression and insomnia, electroacupuncture for 30 minutes 3 times weekly for 8 consecutive weeks resulted in significantly lower insomnia severity scores during the 8-week treatment and the 24-week follow-up periods and significantly lower depression scores using the 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale than either sham acupuncture or standard care consisting of advice on diet, exercise and stress.

Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) uses a magnet to activate the brain. TMS has insufficient evidence to determine its efficacy or recommend clinical indications. Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 small trials with significant heterogeneity, and including 392 patients, found TMS of benefit in early (2 week) response to antidepressant treatment (43.3% vs. 26.8%) but not remission rates; at 6 weeks, both response to treatment and remission demonstrated benefit for TMS (53.8% [57/106] vs. 38.64% [36/107] of subjects receiving active TMS and sham TMS, respectively). rTMS is no better than other interventions.

Magnetic seizure therapy (MST) borrows aspects from both ECT and rTMS. MST uses magnetic pulses to stimulate a precise brain target, but unlike rTMS and similar to ECT, MST aims to induce a seizure but with less subsequent cognitive impairment vs. ECT. In two small open label trials of patients with treatment-resistant depression, MST resulted in a lowered suicide ideation score and remission was seen 46% to 53%.

Real-time functional MRI neurofeedback training to increase the amygdala's hemodynamic response to positive memories was more successful in achieving depression remission than treatment in a parietal control region not involved in emotional processing based on a RCT of 36 patients with depression.
Elderly patients with cognitive impairment who were exposed to light therapy had moderate improvements in depression, as well as improvements in behavioral disturbances and sleep quality.
People who engage in more physical activity are less likely to exhibit depression.

Authors of a meta-analysis found that depressive symptoms decrease in patients with chronic illness who exercise; the response is greater in patients with higher depression scores and in those who exercise regularly.

High- and low-intensity aerobic exercise is effective and recommended for all without contraindications, NNT = 5 for high intensity aerobic exercise, but medication therapy works faster and has less treatment discontinuation. In a Cochrane review of exercise for depression treatment, the effect size, however, was small when considering only the 4 trials with adequate allocation concealment, intention-to-treat analysis and blinded outcome assessment.

For adults with neurologic disorders, a meta-analysis of RCTs found an overall low-moderate effect size of 0.28 (SE .07; 95% CI: 0.15-0.41) favoring an exercise intervention for reducing depression outcomes compared with the control condition.
Structured exercise programs for postpartum women have a small to moderate effect for treatment and prevention of depressive symptoms..

In a RCT of 117 employees sick-listed for a median duration of 4.8 months because of major depression, adjunctive occupational therapy improved depressive symptoms and long-term depression recovery but did not influence work participation.

Successful interventions, based on high-quality data that reduce work disability in employees with depressive disorders include a work-directed intervention added to a clinical intervention, telephone outreach, and online cognitive behavioral therapy.
There is no evidence that massage is effective for treatment of depression.

Improvement in diet through 7 individual dietary support sessions encouraging consumption of whole grains, vegetables, fruit, legumes, low-fat and unsweetened dairy products, raw and unsalted nuts, fish, lean red meats, chicken, eggs, and olive oil in patients with moderate to severe major depression and poor dietary quality increased the rate of clinical remission after 12 weeks (32.3% vs. 8.0% in support only control group; NNT 4.1).
Quitting smoking leads to improvement in anxiety and depression that is similar to the improvement seen following drug treatment.

Implement psychotherapy after considering the following factors: clinical history, symptom severity, risk of suicide, tolerability/safety of medication side effects, patient preference, cost/availability (see and ). Interpersonal therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) are the recommended modalities.

Psychotherapy is equally effective as antidepressant medications after the first 3 months of treatment (see ).
Combination treatment with antidepressant medication and psychotherapy is more effective than either modality alone, NNT = 4.
The mere act of placing patients with depression on a psychotherapy wait list for 6 months may reduce depression symptoms.

In the Netherlands, investigators found a lower response rate to individual psychotherapy (27%) than response rates reported in RCTs (34%-58%); this rate was similar to the response rate to psychotherapy reported in the STAR*D trial (25%). The response rate to combination therapy was also lower than reported in RCTs (21% vs. 45%-63%) and similar to the rate reported in STAR*D (23%).

Authors of a systematic review found equal benefit with CBT or drug therapy with second generation antidepressants in terms of inducing a response or remission but no research on whether relapse is prevented more by one approach or the other. None of the studies included a no-treatment group.
In a systematic review of 20 studies, CBT delivered in primary care settings to patients with anxiety or depression was at least as effective as usual treatment, including medication.
Behavioral activation therapy, a component of CBT which focuses on behaviors associated with depression and behavior change, was noninferior to CBT with respect to depression symptoms in one RCT.

Long-term CBT prevents recurrence, NNT = 1.8. In an RCT of 424 adult patients with three or more previous major depressive episodes who were on a therapeutic dose of maintenance antidepressants, the time to relapse or recurrence of depression did not differ between patients randomized to mindfulness-based cognitive therapy or continued maintenance antidepressants over 24 months. Both therapies were associated with positive effects on recurrence, residual depressive symptoms, and quality of life.
The benefits of combined cognitive and pharmacotherapy over medication alone may be limited to patients with severe, nonchronic depression.

Enhanced depression treatment including problem-solving therapy and/or pharmacotherapy vs. usual care was associated with a reduced risk of death or hospitalization for myocardial infarction/unstable angina during active treatment, but the effects did not persist after treatment ceased by 12 months.

Problem-solving education was beneficial over usual care for reducing the number of depressive symptom elevations in mothers enrolled in Head Start who had depressed mood, anhedonia, or depression history but who did not currently have MDD.
Neurocognitive remediation therapy is undergoing testing as a potential treatment modality for the neurocognitive difficulties that are associated with depression.
Marital therapy may be as effective as individual therapy and antidepressant medication.

Authors of a Cochrane review found couple's therapy was as effective as individual psychotherapy in improving depressive symptoms and more effective in improving relationship distress based on limited evidence.

Among 925 adult depressed patients, a tailored interactive multimedia computer program was more effective than an engagement video for increasing clinician recommendations for antidepressant drugs, a mental health referral, or both. However, there was no effect on mental health at 12-week follow-up.
Music therapy is beneficial for depressive symptoms when added to usual treatment.

A 2020 study of 2,690 smartphone apps relevant to depression and suicide, of which 69 met study inclusion criteria for addressing evidence-based suicide prevention strategies, showed a disturbingly high rate of inaccurate or unhelpful information given to patients using these apps; like all health apps, quality and safety is not regulated or ensured.

Multicomponent collaborative depression care for people with cancer and major depression resulted in an improved treatment response (≥50% reduction in depression score) over usual care (62% vs. 17%, respectively).
Authors of a meta-analysis of home-based supportive care after stroke found a moderate-size effect of this type of care on depressive symptoms.

Counseling for patients with mental health and psychosocial problems in primary care in the UK was associated with improved short-term outcomes and high patient satisfaction but no additional long-term advantages.

Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is at least as effective as medication and may have more rapid effect. In a meta-analysis of 13 studies, the response rate was better for patients randomized to ECT plus antidepressant (RR 1.82; 95% CI: 1.55-2.14) and ECT alone (RR 2.24; 95% CI: 1.51-3.33) compared with antidepressant alone. There were no significant differences in response rate between ECT plus antidepressant and ECT alone, however, ECT plus antidepressant increased the incidence of memory deterioration relative to ECT alone.

ECT should be considered for patients with: risk of harming themselves or others, severe symptoms (e.g., profound functional deterioration, catatonia, psychosis), or contraindications/intolerance/lack of response to antidepressant medications. ECT may cause an elevation of troponin in a small number of patients.
In an RCT of 138 patients with MDD, twice-weekly high-dose unilateral ECT was noninferior to bitemporal ECT for depression with fewer cognitive side-effects.

A 3-year follow-up study of 20 patients following deep brain stimulation (bilateral implantation of electrodes at specific neuroanatomical sites) found average response rates at 1, 2, and 3 years of 62.5%, 46.2%, and 75%, respectively with evidence of continued improvement in physical health and social functioning; there were two patients who died of suicide.
Little is known about the usefulness of watchful waiting compared with antidepressants for the management of subclinical or mild-moderate depression in primary care, as RCTs are lacking.

Care management programs decrease severity better than usual care and should be used whenever their higher cost is not prohibitive. Although integrated care appears to improve depression outcomes, it is not clear how this care should be provided; authors of a meta-analysis found that the degree of integration was not significantly related to depression outcomes.
Collaborative care improves outcomes for patients with symptoms unresponsive to initial medication treatment or history of recurrence.

Among adolescents with depression, collaborative care including an initial in-person engagement session and regular follow-up by master's-level clinicians improved depression response and remission at 12 months over usual care with access to mental health services (67.6% vs. 38.6% for depression response and 50.4% vs. 20.7% for remission, respectively).

Although community engagement and planning across multiple programs improved 6-month mental health scores for minority clients with depressive symptoms and reduced behavioral health hospitalizations compared to provision of technical assistance/resources to individual programs, this difference was not maintained at 12 months.

Treatment is divided into three consecutive phases: acute (from initial presentation to complete remission), continuation (4-9 months of effective treatment dose or psychotherapeutic regimen after remission to prevent relapse), and maintenance (ongoing treatment beyond continuation phase to prevent recurrence) (see ).
Treatment duration of 12 months is supported by evidence from 3 small trials in elderly patients with depression.
Consider maintenance treatment for patients with recurrent or severe depression or high risk of recurrence (see ).

Psychiatric referral is indicated for: severe functional impairment, treatment-resistant symptoms, concomitant psychiatric disorders/symptoms (e.g., eating disorder, alcohol/substance abuse, mania, or psychosis), or suicidal ideation (with or without specific plans; see ).

Emergent psychiatric evaluation is indicated for: suicidal ideation characterized by specific plans, readiness (e.g., possession of objects needed for plan, timeline for plan) or furtherance (active steps taken to prepare for plan); life-threatening behaviors (e.g., not eating, or inability to care for infant in postpartum depression); plans to harm others (e.g., infant in postpartum depression); postpartum psychosis (see ).

The AAP guidelines recommend that adolescents with moderate or severe depression and substance abuse or psychosis should be referred for mental health specialist consultation with ongoing co-management by the primary physician.

Most patients experience long-term subsyndromal symptoms of varying severity for years after a major depressive episode.
Patients with only one lifetime major depressive episode are more likely than patients with recurrence to be free of chronic symptoms subsequent to treatment.

In a Canadian prospective cohort study, 45% of patients with depression had a recurrence in 6 years. Individuals who smoked, felt that they had no control over life's circumstances, and those who had a previous history of depression were more likely to have a recurrence.

Risk of mortality increases in men and possibly women with depression. Based on a total of 3410 adults enrolled in 3 representative samples of a county in Atlantic Canada in 1952, 1970 and 1992, investigators found increased hazard ratios for mortality, ranging from 2.9 in the earliest year to 1.52, among patients with depressed mood and associated symptoms of 1 or more months duration.
Women with perimenopausal depression may experience recurrence of depressive symptoms when discontinuing estrogen treatment.
In a study of adolescents with MDD, suicide attempts over 28 weeks of follow-up were associated with high suicidality, nonsuicidal self-injury, and poor family function at study entry.
Patients treated with psychotherapy require regular monitoring (see ).

Monitor during treatment: suicidality development/progression, symptom severity; functional status; side effect development; adherence; switch to mania; new psychiatric symptoms; general medical conditions.
Acute phase: follow-up visit every 1 to 4 weeks (see and ).
Continuation phase: follow-up visit every month (see and ).
Maintenance phase: follow up visit every 2 to 3 months (see , and ).
Increase monitoring frequency for: suicidality, severe symptoms, problems with treatment adherence, minimal social supports, comorbid general medical problems (see and ).

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidelines recommend systematically tracking symptoms as well as functioning at school, home, and among peers. This monitoring can be aided by use of a tracking tool (e.g., www.gladpc.org).
Same diagnostic criteria as in younger patients.

Start antidepressant medications with half the recommended initial dose, then titrate upward cautiously. SSRIs, TCAs, venlafaxine, and bupropion are equally effective, but TCAs may have higher dropout rates due to side effects.

In a 3-arm RCT of 142 geriatric patients with depression, citalopram plus methylphenidate provided faster improvement of depression symptoms and a higher rate of remission of depression at 4 weeks and 16 weeks than either medication alone.

Authors of a Cochrane review found a statistically significant difference favoring antidepressants in reducing recurrence compared with placebo (three RCTs; N 247; RR 0.67; 95% CI: 0.55-0.82; NNT 5) at 12 months. At 24 months, there was no significant difference for antidepressants overall, however, for the subgroup of geriatric patients using tricyclic antidepressants there was significant benefit in three trials. At 36 months there was no significant difference for antidepressants.
Psychotherapy improves symptoms. Collaborative multidisciplinary treatment is more effective than usual care, NNT= 4.

In a meta-analysis of 8 RCTs on continuation and maintenance of antidepressants in the elderly, the NNT for antidepressants to prevent one additional relapse or recurrence was 3.6 (95% CI: 2.8-4.8). The NNT for TCAs was 2.9 (95% CI: 2.2-4.6) compared with 4.2 for SSRIs (95% CI: 3.2-5.9).
The USPSTF recommends counseling for pregnant women at risk for depression.
Depression screening during pregnancy results in 2.1% to 9.1% absolute reductions in risk of depression at 3 to 5-month follow-up. During pregnancy, use the same criteria for diagnosis.
Depression is associated with increased risk of low birth weight, preterm and small for gestational age births, as well as decreased cognitive ability among offspring.
See chapter on Postpartum depression.

Initial treatment for women experiencing mild to moderate depression during pregnancy or lactation is nonpharmacologic treatment (CBT, interpersonal therapy), although RCTs specifically focusing on the efficacy of these treatments in pregnancy are lacking.

Pooled results from 10 studies on CBT vs. usual care for pregnant and postpartum women with screen-detected depression showed an increase in the likelihood of remission from 6.2% to 34.6% (pooled relative risk 1.34; 95% CI: 1.19-1.50).

Authors of a meta-analysis found a small to moderate effect of exercise for treatment and prevention of depressive symptoms; the most benefit was found for supervised programs for treatment of postpartum depression.

Among women with prior depression who stopped antidepressants during pregnancy, there was a 5 times higher risk of relapse during pregnancy. Maintaining antidepressant medication during pregnancy significantly reduces relapse, NNT = 2.

There is no association between in utero antidepressant exposure and subsequent cognitive dysfunction. There is evidence of an increase in autism spectrum disorder in children whose mothers were exposed to antidepressants in the preconception period (OR 1.77; 95% CI: 1.49-2.09) or in utero (OR 1.52; 95% CI: 1.09-2.12) controlled for past maternal mental illness. Benefits of treatment often outweigh risks; treatment is recommended according to usual guidelines, with exceptions noted below.

SSRIs, except paroxetine (see below), are generally considered safe. However, in a small case-control study, SSRIs taken after 20 weeks gestation were associated with 6x higher risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. In a population-based Danish study of 920,620 births with 12,425 offspring exposed to an SSRI during pregnancy, there was no association between SSRI use and stillbirth or neonatal mortality. Authors of a meta-analysis of 8 observational studies found a slightly increased risk of preterm birth in women taking SSRIs during pregnancy vs. no exposure (11.6% vs. 5.2%; adjusted odds ratio 1.24; 1.09-1.41).
Paroxetine is FDA class D because of increased risk of congenital malformations, particularly cardiac septal defects.

Fluoxetine is best studied and does not lead to increased major malformations or spontaneous abortion. First trimester exposure may lead to increased minor anomalies; 3rd trimester exposure may lead to increased premature delivery, short-term neonatal complications, low birth weight, and shorter birth length. Use of SSRIs in the third trimester has been reported to cause withdrawal symptoms in newborns (e.g., jitteriness, increased muscle tone, irritability, altered sleep patterns, tremors and difficulty eating). (The Organization of Teratology Information Specialists. Fluoxetine. Available at http://www.otispregnancy.org/files/fluoxetine.pdf.)
Pooled estimates for response and remission found that SSRIs were significantly more effective than placebo for women with postpartum depression; quality of evidence, however, was very low.
Bupropion use in pregnancy does not increase malformation risk but may increase risk of spontaneous abortion.
Venlafaxine does not increase major malformation risk.
Breastfeeding while on SSRIs results in some infant exposure via breast milk; sertraline, paroxetine, and most tricyclic antidepressants are considered safe.
Psychological and educational interventions may prevent depression among children and adolescents.
Symptoms are similar to those described for adults, but core symptom may be either depressed or irritable mood; failure to gain weight as expected qualifies as one of the additional required symptoms

For adolescents, AAP guidelines state that mild depression should be handled with watchful waiting as a first step for 6-8 weeks prior to trying psychotherapy or medication. Moderate to severe depression should be treated with psychotherapy and low-dose drug treatment.

The AAP guidelines recommend active support and monitoring with weekly or biweekly visits for 6 to 8 weeks for adolescents with mild depression. For those with moderate or severe depression, or mild depression not responding to initial treatment, consider psychotherapy (cognitive behavioral therapy or interpersonal psychotherapy) and/or antidepressant treatment using low doses of antidepressants with monitoring for adverse effects.

In a study of 187 adolescents requesting depression treatment, a computer fantasy game delivering CBT resulted in similar improvements in depression symptoms over 2 months when compared with usual therapy (mainly counseling).
In conjunction with therapy, fluoxetine may be used in patients age 8 years and older and escitalopram may be used in patients age 12 years and older.

Antidepressant medications are associated with increased risk of suicidal thinking and behavior among children, adolescents, and young adults up to 24 years old. Fluoxetine appears to be the safest SSRI in this population. The Cochrane review on newer generation antidepressant use in adolescents and children found high risk of study bias but confirmed a small reduction in depressive symptoms, higher remission rate (from 380 per 1000 to 448 per 1000), and increased risk of suicide-related outcome (from 25 in 1000 to 40 in 1000).

Authors of a recent meta-analysis of 34 low-quality trials, including 5260 participants and 14 antidepressant treatments, found that only fluoxetine was statistically significantly more effective than placebo for depression in children and adolescents.
TCAs are not effective for children but may have benefit among adolescents.
Among adolescents not responding to initial SSRI, switching to another SSRI is as effective as switching to venlafaxine.

Combining SSRIs with CBT is associated with fewer suicidal events among adolescents when compared to SSRIs alone. CBT and fluoxetine are equally effective in adolescents after 6 months, and 9 months treatment CBT effectively maintains remission during continuation phase.
CBT augmentation may improve depression severity among adolescents not responding to antidepressant medication alone.

In the Youth Depression Alleviation-Combined Treatment RCT of 153 patients, mean age 19.6 years, with moderate to severe MDD, there were no differences between patients randomized to CBT plus fluoxetine and CBT plus placebo at 12 weeks in depression scores, which were reduced in both groups, or in suicide attempts (1 vs. 5, respectively). There were high proportions of participants with anxiety disorder comorbidity (64% and 61%, respectively) and an indication of benefit on anxiety symptoms with active drug treatment.
